# Published knowledge-tracing models under one protocol on three tutor corpora

# Thirteen models and baselines, nine gated on a published number and six with a planted-effect floor that counts, predict the next answer on two Cognitive Tutor logs and on EDM Cup 2023; the attention models AKT and simpleKT have the highest mean AUC on all three, though on half A and EDM Cup their lead over IEKT, fitted there on a GPU, is device-sensitive; and with 2% of the training learners on the two Cognitive Tutor logs, the recurrent deep models lose more than the logistic and attention models, though most of these numbers have no floor at that size.

David S. Porcaro, Learning Design Alliance

Research and writing carried out with Claude Code (Anthropic). See AI use.

# Abstract

Knowledge-tracing models predict a learner's next answer from the answers they have already given. They are usually compared with numbers copied from different papers, each of which prepared its data differently. This study scored thirteen published models and baselines under one protocol, with the same learners, the same test answers and one scorer, on three tutor logs: two from the KDD Cup 2010 Cognitive Tutor data (half A, one half of the learners of Algebra I 2006-07, and Bridge to Algebra 2006-07) and one from EDM Cup 2023. A model's numbers counted only after it passed two checks. Nine models had to reproduce a result published for them, and all nine did, three of them only after a correction. The six deep models also had to let the benchmark detect a practice effect planted in synthetic data shaped like each log. HawkesKT failed this check on both KDD logs, and DKT failed it with 2% of the training learners on half A. Numbers that did not pass both checks are reported but not read as results, except those of item-response theory, the reference, which is exempt from the second check.

Accuracy is measured by AUC, the chance that a model ranks a correct answer above an incorrect one (0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect). # 1. Introduction

A knowledge-tracing model estimates what a learner knows from the record of their answers and predicts their next answer. The field has dozens of such models, from Bayesian knowledge tracing (Corbett & Anderson, 1995) and logistic models of practice (Pavlik, Cen & Koedinger, 2009) to recurrent and attention-based neural networks (Piech et al., 2015; Ghosh, Heffernan & Lan, 2020). Choosing among them for a course, or deciding whether a new model is an improvement, needs comparisons that hold everything except the model fixed.

That condition is rarely met. Published comparisons differ in how rows are built from a tutor's log, whether a step with several skills becomes one row or several, how learners are split into training and test sets, and whether a model sees information from the future of the sequence it predicts. Liu et al. (2022) built a common library and evaluation protocol for deep models so that such choices are made once, for every model. Gervet et al. (2020) compared logistic and deep models on nine corpora under one protocol and found that which family wins depends on the size and shape of the data.

A benchmark is only as good as its instrument, and two checks are seldom made conditions of counting a result. The first is whether each re-implemented model reproduces a published number before its new numbers are trusted. Earlier comparisons have printed the best earlier published value beside their own where one existed (Gervet et al., 2020, Tables 3 to 11), have reproduced a deep model and found that its first reported advantage depended on how the data were formatted (Xiong et al., 2016), and have documented disagreements between reported results (Sarsa, Leinonen & Hellas, 2022). None of those cited here sets a band that a re-implementation must meet before its numbers are used. The second is whether the benchmark can detect, through each model, an effect of known size: a model that loses a learning effect in its input pipeline can still score a respectable AUC, and nothing in the AUC says so. Simulated learners have been used to check single models against a known generating process. A recurrent model's predictions matched those of an oracle on simulated students (Piech et al., 2015); the fitted parameters of Bayesian knowledge tracing have been compared with the parameters that generated simulated data at several sample sizes (Slater & Baker, 2018); and simulated students exposed an implementation error in a tracing model that earlier evaluation had missed (Zhang & MacLellan, 2021). This paper reports a benchmark that makes both checks a condition of counting a number, and reads the published models and baselines through it on three open tutor corpora, at full training data and as training data thins.

# 2. Background

Comparisons under one protocol. Gervet et al. (2020) scored item-response theory (IRT), performance factors analysis (PFA), their "Best-LR" logistic regression and deep knowledge tracing (DKT) on nine corpora with the same folds, and found that logistic models matched or beat deep ones on the smaller corpora, while DKT led on the larger ones. The pyKT library (Liu et al., 2022) re-implemented many deep models with one preprocessing and evaluation protocol and published their AUC on several corpora, including the KDD Cup 2010 files. Its authors' simpleKT (Liu et al., 2023) is a deliberately simple attention model, proposed as a baseline that more complex models find hard to beat under that protocol. Bai et al. (2025) report a further table of the same models under pyKT's protocol, including the time-aware HawkesKT and LPKT.

The models. IRT, in the form Gervet et al. use, predicts from item difficulty alone. PFA adds counts of a learner's earlier successes and failures on each skill (Pavlik, Cen & Koedinger, 2009), and Best-LR adds item and skill difficulties and the counts of all earlier attempts (Gervet et al., 2020). Adding counts within time windows, as DAS3H does (Choffin et al., 2019), gives the variant called Best-LR with time windows here. Gervet et al. (2020, Table 13) fitted a similar addition and found that it added nothing to Best-LR (0.799 against 0.803 on bridge06), and Schmucker et al. (2022) give the name Best-LR+ to a larger extension that also adds recency-weighted and spacing features. Bayesian knowledge tracing (BKT) models each skill as a hidden two-state variable with learning, guessing and slipping probabilities (Corbett & Anderson, 1995). The deep models are DKT, a recurrent network over the answer sequence (Piech et al., 2015); AKT, which attends over earlier answers with a decay in their distance (Ghosh, Heffernan & Lan, 2020); simpleKT (Liu et al., 2023); IEKT, which estimates a learner's cognition and acquisition at each step (Long et al., 2021); HawkesKT, which models the cross-effects of earlier answers as a temporal point process over clock time (Wang et al., 2021); and LPKT, which models learning and forgetting from answer and interval times (Shen et al., 2021). Pelánek (2017) reviews the non-deep families and the questions of evaluation they raise.

What is not established. The published comparisons report AUC. Gervet et al. (2020) print the best earlier published value beside their own where one existed, but none of the comparisons cited here makes reproducing a published number within a set band a condition of reporting a model. None checks, through every model it scores, whether a planted effect of known size reaches the predictions; the simulation studies cited in the introduction check one model at a time. How models degrade as training data thins has been measured for some of them. Gervet et al. (2020, Figure 5) subsampled the training set of one corpus within fixed folds and found Best-LR ahead of DKT below about one million interactions and behind it above. Slater and Baker (2018) measured how far the fitted parameters of Bayesian knowledge tracing fall from those that generated simulated data as the number of students shrinks. No study found here thins logistic, Bayesian and deep models together on the same nested subsets under one protocol.

# 3. Research questions

  • RQ1. Do the benchmark's implementations of the models reproduce the published numbers they are gated on?
  • RQ2. Can the benchmark detect a planted practice effect through each model, with a quarter and with 2% of the training learners?
  • RQ3. With all training learners, how well does each model predict the next answer on each corpus?
  • RQ4. How does each model's prediction change as training data thins, in learners and in history length?

# 4. Method

# 4.1 Corpora, rows and folds

Three spent corpora were used: corpora whose outcomes earlier studies had already read, so that no held-out data was consumed. Bridge06 is the KDD Cup 2010 development training file of Carnegie Learning's Bridge to Algebra 2006-07 tutor (Stamper et al., 2010), built with Gervet et al.'s (2020) preprocessing: one row per learner and step, a skill tag required, duplicate rows dropped, and learners with fewer than ten rows dropped, leaving 1,130 learners. Half A is one of two halves of the learners of the Algebra I 2006-07 file, split by learner with a fixed seed before any outcome was read, with the same preprocessing (635 learners). The other half is reserved for a separate study and was never read. EDM Cup 2023 (Heffernan & Prihar, 2023) is a log of the ASSISTments platform. Its rows are one per learner and problem log, scored on the first response, which counts as correct only if the first action is a correct response; learners with fewer than ten rows were dropped (29,255 learners). Actions are ordered within a problem log by time, with ties broken by file order. No exact duplicate action line was found, so none was dropped.

On the KDD files, the item is the problem and step, and the concept is the step's combination of knowledge components (KCs): every model that takes one concept per row receives the combination, so no step is expanded into one row per KC and no label of a sibling row can leak. Expanding a step into one row per KC repeats its answer across the expanded rows. Xiong et al. (2016) found that sequences repeated once per skill in a public dataset favored DKT, Liu et al. (2022) show that predicting expanded KC sequences one row at a time inflates AUC, and Badran and Preisach (2025) show that a model can learn the correlation between the KCs of one item and so leak its label. Treating each combination as one concept follows Gervet et al. (2020). The logistic models use Gervet et al.'s multi-hot KC encoding. On EDM Cup the item is the problem and the concept its skill code. The rule was to use the sorted combination where a problem carries several codes, but no problem does; the 1,185Printed1,185Source value1185Filecode/studies/models/state-estimator-benchmark/rivals/out/tables.jsonFieldprep › no_code_problemsAnalysistables (release file)Build checkmatches at build problems that carry no code share one "no skill code" concept.

Every corpus is split into five folds by learner (a seeded permutation of the learners cut into five equal parts). In each fold, the test learners' rows are predicted from a model trained on the other learners. Ten percent of the training learners form a selection split that no model trains, tunes or stops on, and the logistic models choose their regularization on a fifth of the remaining training learners. Each learner's first row is kept as history and not scored. The test rows are identical for every model: 850,601 on half A, 1,816,263 on bridge06 and 3,556,155 on EDM Cup, summed over the five folds. Every row is scored, including rows after a learner asked for help; the registration also names unassisted and first-attempt row sets, which this pass did not score.

# 4.2 Models

Table 1 lists the thirteen models and baselines this release reports. The logistic models choose the regularization constant C from {0.1, 1, 10} on each fold's inner learners, with a solver limit of 5,000 iterations; "Best-LR (1,000 iterations)" is the same model at 1,000. The deep models are trained on windows of 200 rows and predict with sliding windows of 200 rows and stride 100, for at most 20 epochs with early stopping on a validation set of 10% of the training learners (patience 2). Each fold screens a grid of four settings (learning rate 10⁻³ or 10⁻⁴, dropout 0.1 or 0.3; on EDM Cup also embedding size 64 or 256, eight settings) for three epochs on its own inner learners, then trains the chosen setting in full. The pyKT models run the pyKT classes at a pinned commit through the benchmark's own training loop. Each deep model is also trained with a second seed on fold 0. The running proportion fits nothing.

The benchmark was registered with a larger roster; this release reports the models in Table 1, and the other models scored under the same protocol are not part of it. DKT2, proposed for an amendment, failed its gate and has no fits. LPKT was added by an amendment after the other stages had been planned and was run on the two KDD corpora only.

# 4.3 Scoring

Every model writes one probability per test row, and one scorer computes every metric from those probabilities: AUC over the fold's test rows, log loss in nats per answer (each probability clipped to [10⁻¹², 1 − 10⁻¹²]), and the share of rows predicted within 10⁻¹² of 0 or 1. No model's own evaluation code produced a reported number. Before any counted run, the benchmark's self-tests confirmed for every model that its prediction for a row does not change when the labels of that row and of every later row are flipped (no future label in the input), and that a deliberately leaking model trips both this test and the floor of section 4.5. Per-row predictions stayed on the machines that made them and were deleted with them; the aggregates are the record.

# 4.4 Gates

A gated model's numbers count only after it reproduces its published number (RQ1). IRT, PFA, Best-LR and DKT were gated on Gervet et al.'s (2020) Table 4 for bridge06: the pooled AUC over five folds on Gervet's rows, first rows included, within ±0.010 of the printed value. The pyKT models were gated in two parts on fold 0 of pyKT's own split of bridge06, with pyKT's preprocessing. First, pyKT's own training loop, scored by pyKT's own evaluation, had to reproduce the published bridge06 AUC within ±0.010 (simpleKT's Table 2 for AKT, simpleKT and IEKT; Bai et al.'s Table 3, a third-party target, for HawkesKT and LPKT). Both tables print means over five folds; the gate reads fold 0. Second, the benchmark's loop, with the same configuration and budget, had to come within ±0.005 of pyKT's loop on the same fold. For this second part, pyKT's loop is scored by pyKT's question-level window AUC, which is computed on the rows the benchmark scores, rather than by pyKT's own evaluation. The two parts therefore read two different AUCs of pyKT's loop, and Table 3 prints both. Four models have no published target of their own on these corpora: BKT, the running proportion, and Best-LR (1,000 iterations) and Best-LR with time windows, which are variants of the gated Best-LR.

# 4.5 The prediction floor

A gate shows that an implementation can reproduce a number; it does not show that the benchmark can see a learning effect through the model (RQ2). The floor, F1, plants one. In a synthetic world built on a corpus's own structure (its learners, items, KC combinations and answer order), each answer is drawn with logit p = α_learner − δ_item + b·log(1 + opportunities on the KC combination), α and δ drawn from a standard normal. The rescaling of the opportunity count by log(1 + x) follows Choffin et al. (2019) and Gervet et al. (2020). Its null twin has the same draws with b = 0. The effect size b was the smallest value in {0.3, 0.45, 0.6, 0.9} at which the oracle's gain over its own ability-and-difficulty part, O, was at least six times its standard error over five twin pairs; b = 0.3 met this on all three corpora.

On fold 0's test rows, with the model trained on 25% (and, separately, 2%) of the training learners of each world, G_E is the model's AUC minus the AUC of the world's ability-and-difficulty probabilities in the effect world, and G_N is the model's AUC minus the oracle's in the null twin. Comparing a model's predictions with those of an oracle in a simulated world follows Piech et al. (2015). A model passes when the 95% interval of G_N does not lie above zero (it cannot beat the true probabilities of a world without practice) and when G_E − G_N has a 95% interval above zero and a point estimate of at least O/2. Intervals come from a learner bootstrap with 2,000 resamples, the same learners resampled across the twin pairs. A model that misses the floor on a corpus reads "not read (floor)" there; one with no floor run reads "no floor run"; and one whose floor was run outside the registered stage lists reads "floor descriptive". IRT is the reference and is exempt.

The registered stage lists named floors for the deep models only: every deep model on every corpus it was fitted on, at 25% and, on half A and EDM Cup, at 2%. The registration gave no other model a floor. Floors for PFA, BKT and the running proportion on the two KDD corpora at 25% were added on the author's decision on 16 November 2026, after the registered fits had run, outside the registered stage lists and under no amendment. They use the registered generator, effect size, bar and pass rule. Their results are reported as descriptive only: Table 4 prints them, but they are not read as passes, so the numbers of these three models are descriptive, like those of a model with no floor run. No floor was run for the Best-LR models.

# 4.6 Regimes

To see how each model behaves as data thins (RQ4), each model was also trained on 25%, 10% and 2% of each fold's training learners, with the test learners unchanged. The 10% and 2% subsets were drawn five times, nested (each 2% draw inside a 10% draw inside the 25% set) and seeded, with the same draws for every model. At 10% and 2%, each model's tuning choices were frozen at its 25% choice for that fold. Separately, every training learner's history was cut to its first 50 or first 20 answers, the test learners keeping theirs whole.

# 4.7 Design history and what this pass can say

The protocol was registered on 11 November 2026, before any counted run. The registration and its amendments are not published yet, because they also govern models this release does not report. Their full text will be published when those models are reported. Until then, the SHA-256 of each document, as it stood when it was last changed, is given below, so that a reader can check later that the published text is the one this benchmark ran under. This section states what they contain.

Four amendments were written while the benchmark ran, between 11 and 15 November 2026. Amendment 1 (11 and 12 November) read PFA against a corrected target (section 5.1). It also built the pyKT gate of section 4.4, which the registration had left unbuilt, and ran pyKT's own loop for that gate on a GPU. Amendment 2 (12 and 13 November) added LPKT. Amendment 3 (13 to 15 November) moved the rented jobs onto machines that each ran several, and recorded the move of some fits to GPUs described below. Amendment 4 (13 to 15 November) rebuilt HawkesKT as pyKT sets it up, after its first gate failed, and was put in force for HawkesKT on 13 November. Amendments 1 to 3 were drafts while the fits ran: each was written under a decision of the author and states that it is not in force until accepted. The author confirmed on 20 November 2026, after the fits, that they are the amendments the benchmark ran under. LPKT's first gate also failed, and its architecture was then tuned on the gate's split before the gate was passed (section 5.1).

The registration pinned every fit to a CPU. Under deviations recorded in Amendment 3, AKT, simpleKT and IEKT on EDM Cup, IEKT on half A and LPKT on both KDD corpora ran on GPUs; every other fit ran on a CPU. The device each fit ran on is recorded in the per-case outputs, and the device control registered for the GPU fits is reported in section 7.2.

The registration also states readings that compare pairs of models with a paired learner bootstrap on the selection split. No comparison job was built for this pass: per-row predictions were not kept, so no paired interval can be computed. Every AUC in this paper is therefore descriptive, and no difference between two models was tested. The registration's questions about named learning-science constructs, read on simulated learners, are outside this release.

Several other registered reports were not made in this pass, and they are listed here so that their absence is not read as a null result. The share of deep fits that stopped at the 20-epoch cap was to be reported per model and corpus, and a model that stopped at the cap on more than half its folds was to be reported as a floor, not a result. The benchmark's committed aggregates do not record each fit's stopping epoch, so neither the shares nor that rule could be applied, and any deep model's status could change under it. For EDM Cup, the registration asked for a sensitivity run that drops the problem logs whose file order disagrees with the time order; it was not made, because it needs new fits. The strata the registration names (rows on items with little training support, a learner's first five answers on a skill, rows with several skills, and rows after help) and the unassisted and first-attempt row sets need per-row predictions, which were not kept. The t interval over the five twin pairs that the registration places beside each floor interval needs each pair's statistic, which the floor's aggregate does not record. The counts of EDM Cup's preprocessing that the registration asks for are given in section 4.1.

# 5. Results

The results answer the four questions in order. Each number is computed from the per-case outputs, one record per scored fit, floor or gate; Tables 2 to 6 print them rounded once from the unrounded values.

Answer to RQ1. Yes, for all nine gated models: each reproduced its published target within the band, PFA only against the target of a second table of the source paper, and HawkesKT and LPKT only after changes made in response to a first failure.

Download the notebook and download the data file (per-case-outputs.jsonl.gz) into the same folder, then run all cells. Python 3.9 or later with numpy.

Re-run: reproductions of published numbers (RQ1)

The per-case outputs (per-case-outputs.jsonl, published with the release) hold one gate record per reproduction, with the benchmark's value, the published target and, for the pyKT models, pyKT's own loop. This notebook recomputes every number of Tables 2 and 3 from those records and checks it against the article. It needs only the standard library.

# Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "knowledge-tracing-benchmark-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = 'per-case-outputs.jsonl'     # this release's per-case file, set when the report is built (None: it has none)


def find_release_file(name=None):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    name = name or DATA_NAME
    if not name:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Release {RELEASE_ID} publishes no per-case file; this notebook reads its "
                                f"code package (code_dir).")
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
        gz = d / (name + ".gz")
        if gz.is_file():
            # The report offers the data file gzipped; unpack it once beside the download, so a notebook that
            # opens the file as text reads the same bytes either way.
            try:
                (d / name).write_bytes(gzip.decompress(gz.read_bytes()))
                return d / name
            except OSError:
                return gz
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def is_this_release(d):
    """True when folder d holds this release, not another one's code/ found higher up: d is named after the
    release, or its code-manifest.txt or a release file (*.yaml) names it."""
    if d.name == RELEASE_ID:
        return True
    texts = [d / "code-manifest.txt", *sorted(d.glob("*.yaml"))]
    return any(f.is_file() and RELEASE_ID in f.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore") for f in texts)


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder), looked for only by a notebook that reads it: in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file() and is_this_release(d):
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


print("Data:", shown(find_release_file()))
Data: per-case-outputs.jsonl

recs = [json.loads(x) for x in open(find_release_file("per-case-outputs.jsonl"), encoding="utf-8")]
gates = [r for r in recs if r["record"] == "gate" and r["attempt"] == "counted"]
first = [r for r in recs if r["record"] == "gate" and r["attempt"] != "counted"]
f4 = lambda x: f"{x:.4f}".replace("-", "−")
s4 = lambda x: f"{x:+.4f}".replace("-", "−")

# Table 2: Gervet et al. (2020) targets, band 0.010
want2 = {("IRT", "gervet"): ("0.7432", "−0.0058", "PASS"),
         ("PFA", "gervet"): ("0.7571", "+0.0161", "HARNESS_FAIL"),
         ("PFA", "gervet-amended"): ("0.7571", "−0.0039", "PASS"),
         ("Best-LR", "gervet"): ("0.8046", "+0.0016", "PASS"),
         ("DKT", "gervet"): ("0.7980", "+0.0080", "PASS")}
for g in gates:
    if g["kind"].startswith("gervet"):
        diff = g["bench_auc"] - g["target"]
        reading = "PASS" if abs(diff) <= 0.010 else "HARNESS_FAIL"
        got = (f4(g["bench_auc"]), s4(diff), reading)
        print(g["model"], g["kind"], g["target"], got)
        assert got == want2[(g["model"], g["kind"])]
print("Table 2 matches the article.")

# Table 3: pyKT gate, reproduction band 0.010 and loop band 0.005
want3 = {"AKT": ("0.8136", "−0.0072", "+0.0030"), "simpleKT": ("0.8111", "−0.0049", "+0.0026"),
         "IEKT": ("0.8052", "−0.0073", "−0.0033"), "HawkesKT": ("0.8028", "−0.0040", "−0.0038"),
         "LPKT": ("0.7980", "−0.0076", "+0.0016")}
for g in gates:
    if g["kind"] == "pykt":
        rep = g["pykt_primary_auc"] - g["target"]
        loop = g["bench_auc"] - g["pykt_loop_auc"]
        assert abs(rep - g["repro_diff"]) < 1e-12 and abs(loop - g["loop_diff"]) < 1e-12
        ok = abs(rep) <= 0.010 and abs(loop) <= 0.005
        got = (f4(g["pykt_primary_auc"]), s4(rep), s4(loop))
        print(g["model"], g["target"], got, "PASS" if ok else "FAIL")
        assert got == want3[g["model"]] and ok and g["reading"] == "PASS"

# 5.2 RQ2: the prediction floor

The floor asks whether the benchmark, through each model, recovers at least half of a practice effect planted in a world shaped like the corpus. Table 4. The prediction floor F1: G_E − G_N with its 95% interval (learner bootstrap, 2,000 resamples, five twin pairs), with the model trained on 25% or 2% of the training learners. Bars O/2: 0.0063 (half A), 0.0085 (bridge06), 0.0065 (EDM Cup). Bold marks the three misses; every other cell of the six deep models passes. The rows of PFA, BKT and the running proportion, whose floors were run outside the registered stage lists (section 4.5), are descriptive only and are not read as passes. In every cell G_N's interval lies below zero. The 2% floor was not run on bridge06.

Every deep model passed the floor at 25% except HawkesKT on the two KDD corpora, where its G_E − G_N was negative (−0.0481Printed−0.0481Source value-0.0481265Filecode/studies/models/state-estimator-benchmark/rivals/out/tables.jsonFieldfloors › HawkesKT › kddcup2010-algebra0607:halfA › quarter › G_E_minus_G_NAnalysistables (release file)Build checkmatches at build on half A and −0.0460Printed−0.0460Source value-0.0459535Filecode/studies/models/state-estimator-benchmark/rivals/out/tables.jsonFieldfloors › HawkesKT › kddcup2010-bridge06 › quarter › G_E_minus_G_NAnalysistables (release file)Build checkmatches at build on bridge06): in the effect world it predicted worse, relative to the world's own probabilities, than in the null world. HawkesKT passed on EDM Cup at both sizes and on half A at 2%. At 2%, DKT missed on half A (−0.0008Printed−0.0008Source value-0.000803827Filecode/studies/models/state-estimator-benchmark/rivals/out/tables.jsonFieldfloors › DKT › kddcup2010-algebra0607:halfA › fiftieth › G_E_minus_G_NAnalysistables (release file)Build checkmatches at build, its interval covering zero) and passed on EDM Cup; the other deep models passed at 2% wherever the floor was run. The floor statistics of PFA, BKT and the running proportion lay above the bar on both KDD corpora, but those floors were run outside the registered stage lists and are reported as descriptive only, not as passes. No model read above zero in a null world, so none showed a sign of reading labels it should not have.

Answer to RQ2. For five of the six deep models given the floor, yes: the benchmark recovered at least half of the planted effect through them at 25% of the training learners on every corpus where the floor was run. Through HawkesKT it did not on either KDD corpus, so HawkesKT's KDD numbers are not read, and through DKT it did not at 2% on half A. The floors of PFA, BKT and the running proportion, run on the KDD corpora outside the registered plan, are descriptive only, and so are those three models' numbers. The three Best-LR models had no floor run, and their numbers are also reported as descriptive only.

Re-run this finding Recompute Table 4, the prediction floor, from the per-case outputs (executed when this report was built; every assertion passed)

Download the notebook and download the data file (per-case-outputs.jsonl.gz) into the same folder, then run all cells. Python 3.9 or later with numpy.

Re-run: the prediction floor (RQ2)

Each floor record holds, for one model, corpus and training size, the oracle's effect-minus-null difference O, G_N with its interval and G_E - G_N with its interval, as the benchmark's scorer wrote them from five synthetic twin pairs. This notebook re-applies the pass rule (G_N's interval not above zero; G_E - G_N's interval above zero with a point estimate of at least O/2), checks it against the scorer's reading, and checks Table 4's printed values and the bars O/2. It needs only the standard library.

The floors of PFA, BKT and the running proportion were run outside the registered stage lists. Their readings are checked here like every other, but the article reports them as descriptive only, not as passes; the floors that count are the six deep models'.

# Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "knowledge-tracing-benchmark-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = 'per-case-outputs.jsonl'     # this release's per-case file, set when the report is built (None: it has none)


def find_release_file(name=None):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    name = name or DATA_NAME
    if not name:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Release {RELEASE_ID} publishes no per-case file; this notebook reads its "
                                f"code package (code_dir).")
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
        gz = d / (name + ".gz")
        if gz.is_file():
            # The report offers the data file gzipped; unpack it once beside the download, so a notebook that
            # opens the file as text reads the same bytes either way.
            try:
                (d / name).write_bytes(gzip.decompress(gz.read_bytes()))
                return d / name
            except OSError:
                return gz
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def is_this_release(d):
    """True when folder d holds this release, not another one's code/ found higher up: d is named after the
    release, or its code-manifest.txt or a release file (*.yaml) names it."""
    if d.name == RELEASE_ID:
        return True
    texts = [d / "code-manifest.txt", *sorted(d.glob("*.yaml"))]
    return any(f.is_file() and RELEASE_ID in f.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore") for f in texts)


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder), looked for only by a notebook that reads it: in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file() and is_this_release(d):
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


print("Data:", shown(find_release_file()))
Data: per-case-outputs.jsonl

recs = [json.loads(x) for x in open(find_release_file("per-case-outputs.jsonl"), encoding="utf-8")]
floors = [r for r in recs if r["record"] == "floor"]
s4 = lambda x: f"{x:+.4f}".replace("-", "−")
for r in floors:
    lo, hi = r["G_E_minus_G_N_ci95"]
    ok = r["G_N_ci95"][1] <= 0 and lo > 0 and r["G_E_minus_G_N"] >= r["O"] / 2
    assert ("PASS" if ok else "MISS") == r["reading"], r
    assert r["G_N_ci95"][1] < 0
print(len(floors), "floor records; the pass rule reproduces every reading; every G_N interval lies below zero.")

        f"{s4(r['G_E_minus_G_N'])} [{s4(r['G_E_minus_G_N_ci95'][0])}, {s4(r['G_E_minus_G_N_ci95'][1])}]" for r in floors}

misses = sorted(k for k in cell if cell[k].startswith("−"))
assert [r for r in floors if r["reading"] == "MISS"].__len__() == 3
O = {}
for r in floors:

DESCRIPTIVE = {"PFA", "BKT", "running-proportion"}
counted = [r for r in floors if r["model"] not in DESCRIPTIVE]

missed25 = {r["model"] for r in counted if r["regime"] == "quarter" and r["reading"] == "MISS"}

half = {k: f"{v / 2:.4f}" for k, v in O.items()}

Table 5. Test AUC with all training learners: the mean over five folds, with the lowest and highest fold in brackets. Bold marks the highest mean on each corpus. Floor status from Table 4 at 25%; numbers marked "not read", "floor descriptive" or "no floor run" are descriptive only under the registered rule. All rows scored (half A 850,601, bridge06 1,816,263, EDM Cup 3,556,155).

Answer to RQ3. The two attention models, AKT and then simpleKT, predicted best on average on all three corpora, by margins small enough that their fold ranges overlap; on half A the logistic model Best-LR with time windows was within 0.0026Printed0.0026Source value0.00260203Filecode/studies/models/state-estimator-benchmark/rivals/out/tables.jsonFieldsummary › halfA_top3 › spreadAnalysistables (release file)Build checkmatches at build of AKT. On EDM Cup the order of AKT, simpleKT and IEKT is device-sensitive, and on half A so is the lead of AKT, simpleKT and Best-LR with time windows over IEKT. Recurrent DKT trailed the logistic Best-LR on the KDD corpora and led it on EDM Cup. These are descriptions of means: no difference between two models was tested.

Re-run this finding Recompute Tables 5 and 6, prediction with all training learners, from the per-case outputs (executed when this report was built; every assertion passed)

Download the notebook and download the data file (per-case-outputs.jsonl.gz) into the same folder, then run all cells. Python 3.9 or later with numpy.

Re-run: prediction with all training learners (RQ3)

The fit records with regime: "main" are each model's five folds with all training learners. This notebook recomputes Table 5 (mean test AUC over the folds, with the lowest and highest fold), Table 6 (mean log loss), the fold counts and the seed difference the text cites. It needs only the standard library.

In the per-case outputs, the model the article calls Best-LR with time windows has the identifier Best-LR+.

# Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "knowledge-tracing-benchmark-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = 'per-case-outputs.jsonl'     # this release's per-case file, set when the report is built (None: it has none)


def find_release_file(name=None):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    name = name or DATA_NAME
    if not name:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Release {RELEASE_ID} publishes no per-case file; this notebook reads its "
                                f"code package (code_dir).")
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
        gz = d / (name + ".gz")
        if gz.is_file():
            # The report offers the data file gzipped; unpack it once beside the download, so a notebook that
            # opens the file as text reads the same bytes either way.
            try:
                (d / name).write_bytes(gzip.decompress(gz.read_bytes()))
                return d / name
            except OSError:
                return gz
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def is_this_release(d):
    """True when folder d holds this release, not another one's code/ found higher up: d is named after the
    release, or its code-manifest.txt or a release file (*.yaml) names it."""
    if d.name == RELEASE_ID:
        return True
    texts = [d / "code-manifest.txt", *sorted(d.glob("*.yaml"))]
    return any(f.is_file() and RELEASE_ID in f.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore") for f in texts)


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder), looked for only by a notebook that reads it: in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file() and is_this_release(d):
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


print("Data:", shown(find_release_file()))

Table 7. Change in mean test AUC from the fits with all training learners, by training regime: 25%, 10% and 2% of the training learners (the 10% and 2% means over five draws and five folds, the others over five folds), and every training learner's history cut to its first 50 or 20 answers (test learners whole). Rows marked "not read" are descriptive only, and so are the rows of the logistic models, BKT and the running proportion, which have no floor that counts (Table 5). At 2%, only the deep models on half A and on EDM Cup had a floor at that size, and DKT missed it on half A ("not read (floor)"); so the 2% cells of AKT, simpleKT, IEKT and LPKT on half A and of DKT, AKT, simpleKT, IEKT and HawkesKT on EDM Cup count, and every other 2% cell is descriptive. The running proportion fits nothing, so it does not change.

Figure 2. Change in mean test AUC from the fits with all training learners, with 2% of the training learners (circles) and with training histories cut to the first 20 answers (squares), per model and corpus. Hollow marks are descriptive only (for 2%, no floor passed at that size; for 20 answers, the model's floor status in Table 5); IRT, the reference, is drawn filled. Source: the per-case outputs (Table 7).

Answer to RQ4. Every model that learns from the training learners lost accuracy as they thinned. With 2% of them, the recurrent deep models lost more than the logistic models on the KDD corpora, the attention models about as much as the Best-LR models, and, of the models that fit anything, BKT least on every corpus; on EDM Cup the ranges of the deep and the logistic models overlapped. With histories cut to twenty answers, the logistic models lost more than the attention models and BKT on the KDD corpora; the logistic models' and BKT's numbers are descriptive only. For each model and corpus, Table 7 is the mean test AUC of a regime's fits (five folds; at 10% and 2%, five draws of five folds) minus the mean of the five fits with all training learners, computed before rounding. # Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "knowledge-tracing-benchmark-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = 'per-case-outputs.jsonl'     # this release's per-case file, set when the report is built (None: it has none)


def find_release_file(name=None):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    name = name or DATA_NAME
    if not name:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Release {RELEASE_ID} publishes no per-case file; this notebook reads its "
                                f"code package (code_dir).")
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
        gz = d / (name + ".gz")
        if gz.is_file():
            # The report offers the data file gzipped; unpack it once beside the download, so a notebook that
            # opens the file as text reads the same bytes either way.
            try:
                (d / name).write_bytes(gzip.decompress(gz.read_bytes()))
                return d / name
            except OSError:
                return gz
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def is_this_release(d):
    """True when folder d holds this release, not another one's code/ found higher up: d is named after the
    release, or its code-manifest.txt or a release file (*.yaml) names it."""
    if d.name == RELEASE_ID:
        return True
    texts = [d / "code-manifest.txt", *sorted(d.glob("*.yaml"))]
    return any(f.is_file() and RELEASE_ID in f.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore") for f in texts)


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder), looked for only by a notebook that reads it: in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file() and is_this_release(d):
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


print("Data:", shown(find_release_file()))
Data: per-case-outputs.jsonl

def rng(cells):
    v = [loss(*x) for x in cells]
    return f"{min(v):.3f}", f"{max(v):.3f}"
DEEP = ["DKT", "AKT", "simpleKT", "IEKT", "HawkesKT", "LPKT"]

edm = [(m, "EDM Cup", "history-twenty") for (m, cc, g) in by if cc == C["EDM Cup"] and g == "main" and m != "running-proportion"]

# 6. Discussion

The benchmark's two checks did work that the AUC could not. The gates caught a model that would otherwise have entered with a training loop 0.157Printed0.157Source value-0.156782Filecode/studies/models/state-estimator-benchmark/rivals/out/tables.jsonFieldgates_first › 0 › loop_diffAnalysistables (release file)Build checkmatches at build AUC below its reference implementation (HawkesKT), a published target whose two printed values disagree, the earlier published value agreeing with the one the benchmark failed (PFA), and a model that needed tuning before it reproduced its source (LPKT). The floor then showed that, even after HawkesKT's gate passed, the benchmark could not recover a planted practice effect through it on the KDD corpora at 25% of the training learners, while it could through every other deep model. A benchmark without a floor would have printed HawkesKT's KDD numbers beside the others with nothing to mark them. Simulated students have exposed an implementation error in a tracing model that its authors' earlier evaluation had not found (Zhang & MacLellan, 2021); the floor makes that check a condition of counting any model's numbers.

The ordering at full data agrees in its main lines with published tables. Under pyKT's protocol, AKT has the highest AUC of the baselines on the two KDD Cup 2010 files of Bai et al.'s (2025) Table 3 (Algebra 2005-06 and Bridge to Algebra 2006-07), and in Gervet et al.'s (2020) Table 4 Best-LR (0.803Printed0.803Source value0.803Filecode/studies/models/state-estimator-benchmark/rivals/out/tables.jsonFieldgates › 3 › targetAnalysistables (release file)Build checkmatches at build) is above DKT (0.790Printed0.790Source value0.79Filecode/studies/models/state-estimator-benchmark/rivals/out/tables.jsonFieldgates › 4 › targetAnalysistables (release file)Build checkmatches at build) on bridge06, as it is here. Other comparisons found logistic, IRT-based or extended Bayesian models matching or beating recurrent ones (Wilson et al., 2016; Khajah, Lindsey & Mozer, 2016; Mandalapu, Gong & Chen, 2021). pyKT's authors found that most later deep models did not beat DKT but that AKT outperformed almost all of them (Liu et al., 2022), as it does here, though on half A and EDM Cup its lead over IEKT is device-sensitive (section 7.2); simpleKT, which they proposed later, is close behind it here. Under this protocol the margins at the top are small: the three highest means on half A (AKT, simpleKT and Best-LR with time windows) lie within 0.0026Printed0.0026Source value0.00260203Filecode/studies/models/state-estimator-benchmark/rivals/out/tables.jsonFieldsummary › halfA_top3 › spreadAnalysistables (release file)Build checkmatches at build of one another, and their lead over IEKT there is device-sensitive (section 7.2). Here Best-LR with time windows read above Best-LR on every corpus, which Gervet et al. (2020, Table 13) did not find for a similar addition; these numbers have no floor. The order changes with the amount of training data, and the two kinds of thinning act differently: fewer learners hurt the recurrent deep models more than the logistic models, the attention models and BKT on the KDD corpora, as Gervet et al. (2020, Figure 5) found for DKT against Best-LR when they subsampled one corpus, while the attention models lost about as much as the Best-LR models. Shorter training histories hurt the logistic models, which count earlier attempts, and the recurrent deep models more than the attention models and BKT on the KDD corpora. The logistic models' and BKT's numbers are descriptive only, and most of the 2% numbers have no floor at that size.

# Implications for practice

A model chosen for a course should be chosen for the amount of data the course will have (RQ4). With all the training learners of these corpora (hundreds to tens of thousands of learners), the attention models AKT and simpleKT predicted best, with a time-windowed logistic model close behind on one corpus (RQ3). Where training learners are few, BKT lost the least accuracy of the models that fit anything and, on the two Cognitive Tutor corpora, the recurrent deep models lost more than the logistic models, the attention models and BKT, while the attention models and the Best-LR models lost about as much as each other (RQ4); most of those small-data numbers had no floor. A re-implemented model's numbers deserve trust only after it has reproduced a published result and shown that it can recover a known effect in data shaped like the course's (RQ1, RQ2).

# Implications for research

Benchmarks of knowledge tracing should report, for each model, a reproduction of a published number and a floor that plants a known effect in data with the corpus's structure, with evidence that the planted world resembles the corpus (Käser & Alexandron, 2024), and should keep per-row predictions so that differences between models can be given paired intervals. Seeds and hardware alone move the results of deep models (Sarsa, Leinonen & Hellas, 2022), so a benchmark should also report them. This pass did not keep them, and that is its main limit. Three questions are open: why the benchmark could not recover the planted effect through HawkesKT on the KDD corpora when it could on EDM Cup; why LPKT on half A lost most of its accuracy at 25% of the training learners; and why the benchmark's PFA reads above both of Gervet et al.'s values and above the 0.739 of Choffin et al. (2019), which only a comparison of the feature construction, or the source paper's authors, can settle. The comparisons on unassisted and first-attempt rows, and the paired comparisons the registration names, need a pass that keeps predictions.

# 7. Threats to validity

# 7.1 Construct validity

AUC over all rows rewards a model for ranking every answer, including answers given after a learner asked for help, which a tutor log records differently from unassisted answers. The registration names unassisted and first-attempt row sets as well; this pass scored all rows only, so its rankings may differ from those on unassisted or first answers.

AUC over all rows also mixes a learner's first attempts on a skill, where models differ most, with later attempts, where they differ much less (Zhang et al., 2021).

The floor plants one form of practice effect, logarithmic in the opportunities on a KC combination. A model that represents practice in another form can miss it while predicting real data well, and a model that passes it has shown only that this form reaches the prediction through it. Bayesian knowledge tracing fitted to data generated by other models of learning can return parameters that contradict its own assumptions (Doroudi & Brunskill, 2017), so a floor in one generating form says little about others.

# 7.2 Internal validity

The deep models' configurations were chosen from small grids on each fold's inner learners, starting from pyKT's published configuration for the nearest pyKT corpus (Algebra I 2005-06 for half A, Bridge to Algebra 2006-07 for bridge06 and ASSISTments 2009 for EDM Cup). A larger search could change any deep model's numbers, and the logistic models had a three-value grid. LPKT's architecture was tuned on bridge06's gate split, a fold whose learners also appear in the benchmark's bridge06 folds, so its bridge06 numbers are not independent of that tuning.

Several deep fits ran on GPUs and the rest on CPUs, and a deep model's fit can differ between devices (Sarsa, Leinonen & Hellas, 2022, measured how much random seeding and hardware alone move such results). The device is recorded per fit, and a device control was registered before the GPU fits counted. For IEKT, AKT and simpleKT, a fixed sample of fits already scored on a CPU was run again once on the GPU type that ran the model's counted fits; for LPKT, two counted GPU fits were run again on a CPU. The samples were not all drawn from the corpora of the counted GPU fits. IEKT's eight are bridge06 fits (three with all training learners, two at 25% and three with histories cut to twenty answers), while its counted GPU fits are on half A and EDM Cup; AKT's and simpleKT's nine each are fits with all training learners on half A (four) and bridge06 (five), while their counted GPU fits are on EDM Cup; LPKT's two are its own counted fits, one on each KDD corpus. The per-case outputs record each fit's device as CPU or GPU, not the GPU type. A model's band is the largest absolute difference in AUC between the two devices over its sample: 0.0169 for IEKT (eight fits, on an NVIDIA RTX A5000), 0.0035 for AKT and 0.0021 for simpleKT (nine fits each, on an NVIDIA A40), and 0.0003 for LPKT (two fits, on an A40). IEKT's band is set by two fits with training histories cut to twenty answers; its other six differences were at most 0.0011. LPKT's band rests on two fits with all training learners, so it may understate the difference in the small-data regimes.

Under the registered rule, a comparison involving one of these models whose margin lies within twice the model's band is reported as device-sensitive. That covers the order of AKT, simpleKT and IEKT on EDM Cup (section 5.3), every comparison in Table 5 between IEKT and a model within 0.034 of it on half A or EDM Cup (among them the lead of AKT, simpleKT and Best-LR with time windows over IEKT on half A), IEKT's 2% loss on EDM Cup against the Best-LR models' (section 5.4), IEKT's 20-answer loss on half A against PFA's and the Best-LR models' (section 5.4), and, on half A, the difference between LPKT and Best-LR (1,000 iterations) (0.0005). The rule marks a comparison; it does not change the numbers.

# 7.3 External validity

Two of the three corpora are halves of one competition's Cognitive Tutor logs from 2006-07, and the third is one platform's log. They are spent corpora that earlier studies had read, chosen so that no held-out data was used. The results are about these three corpora and this protocol; on other tutors, other row definitions or other splits the order may change. LPKT was not fitted on EDM Cup.

# 7.4 Statistical conclusion validity

No difference between two models was tested, because no per-row predictions were kept. The fold ranges in Table 5 are not confidence intervals, and the fold counts in section 5.3 are descriptions. A difference of 0.002 between two means here may or may not exceed the paired uncertainty, which is unknown.

The floors for the three Best-LR models were not run, and for PFA, BKT and the running proportion they were not run on EDM Cup; those run for these three on the KDD corpora were added after the registered fits, outside the registered stage lists (section 4.5), and are reported as descriptive only. Under the registered rule every number of the three Best-LR models, PFA, BKT and the running proportion is therefore descriptive only. The 2% floor was not run on bridge06, so no 2% number on bridge06 has a floor.

# 7.5 Conflict of interest

The benchmark was built to establish how well published knowledge-tracing models perform under one protocol, as a baseline for a new, publicly available model that the author's program is developing. That model is not reported in this release, nor are other models the author's program scored for its own reference, some of which it develops. The author works with the Learning Design Alliance (LDA), which, besides this research, builds learning authoring software. The protocol was registered before any counted run, though the registration is not published (section 4.7), and the per-fit aggregates are published with this release.

# 8. Conclusion

Under one protocol, thirteen published knowledge-tracing models and baselines were scored on three tutor corpora; nine were gated on a published number, and the six deep models were given a planted-effect floor. All nine gated models reproduced a published number, three of them only after a correction, and the floor showed that the benchmark could not read a practice effect through HawkesKT on the two KDD corpora, or through DKT with 2% of the training learners on half A. With all training learners the attention models AKT and simpleKT had the highest mean AUC on every corpus, closely followed on one corpus by a time-windowed logistic model. On half A and EDM Cup their lead over IEKT, whose fits there ran on a GPU, lies within twice IEKT's device band, so under the registered rule it is device-sensitive.

The order is not fixed. With 2% of the training learners the recurrent deep models lost more than the logistic models, the attention models and BKT on the two Cognitive Tutor corpora, and of the models that fit anything BKT lost least on every corpus, while the attention models lost about as much as the Best-LR models; most of these numbers have no floor at that size. With short histories the logistic models lost more than the attention models and BKT on the two Cognitive Tutor corpora; the logistic models' and BKT's numbers are descriptive only. The model to use therefore depends on the data a course will have. A benchmark that wants to say more than this needs to keep its predictions, so that differences can be given intervals.

# 9. Data, code and provenance

Data. No corpus is redistributed. The KDD Cup 2010 files are obtained from the PSLC DataShop (https://pslcdatashop.web.cmu.edu/KDDCup/) under DataShop's terms, and EDM Cup 2023 from OSF (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/YRWUH) under the ASSISTments Data Terms of Use. The release file records each file read with its SHA-256 hash. In the per-case outputs, the summary tables and the code, the model identifier Best-LR+ (Best-LRplus in job identifiers) denotes Best-LR with time windows, and Best-LR-iter1000 denotes Best-LR (1,000 iterations).

This is version 1.0.1 of the release. It corrects the abstract and the conflict-of-interest statement of version 1.0.0 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24481646), which stays as published; no analysis, number or verdict changed.

What is not published, and why. The benchmark's fitting harness (the model adapters, the rented-machine runner and the stage lists) is not in the code package, because it also carries models this release does not report; the per-fit aggregates it produced are published, and every number in this paper can be recomputed from them, but the fits themselves cannot be rerun from the package. The per-row predictions were never kept. The registration (11 November 2026) and its four amendments (written from 11 to 15 November 2026) are not published yet, because they also govern models this release does not report; their SHA-256 fingerprints are in section 4.7, and their full text will be published when those models are reported. Section 4 states every rule this release applies, and section 4.7 the departures from them.

# AI use

I, David Porcaro, conducted this study with a Claude Code process that included reviewing past research, writing the code, splitting the data, commissioning and managing externally rented CPUs and GPUs, analyzing the results and writing up the report. I do not take claim for work I did not do.

I did select the research study, the questions, the models, and the datasets. I reviewed and approved all proposed plans, reviewing results as they came in, managed the prioritization of available computer resources, reviewed all interim results as they came in, and reviewed and approved all amendments. I reviewed the final report, provided suggested edits, and conducted a tell-back quiz to ensure I understood the headline changes. I am ultimately responsible for the research process.

# Reviews and the record

Specialist reviews requested

These reviews are post-publication: the release goes out with them named, and each attaches as a review record when done.

  • psychometrician or knowledge-tracing methodologist: the prediction floor (a logarithmic practice effect planted on each corpus's structure, read against null twins) is a valid detection floor for a model's ability to carry a practice effect into its predictions
  • deep knowledge-tracing practitioner: the pyKT gate (pyKT's own loop against the published value, then the benchmark loop against pyKT's loop on one fold) establishes that the deep implementations are faithful

Review records filed against this release

  • None filed yet.

To add one, use Review beside any paragraph: it drafts a record in the learning-wiki review schema for you to submit.
